120.title: Om jai jagadish hare
120.carry: victory to the lord of the world
120.howItsDone: In many Hindu homes and temples, especially in North India and the diaspora, Om jai jagadish hare is sung while the arti lamp is circled at the end of puja, with a bell ringing and everyone joining in.

segments.voice: Yesterday, arti at home: a small flame, circled clockwise. Your line was light, circled. What did you notice yourself circling back to? Day one hundred and twenty.

Ask almost anyone who grew up in a North Indian Hindu family to hum the arti song, and watch what happens. They'll roll their eyes, then start, and then they won't be able to stop. It's the tune from every birthday puja, every housewarming, every Diwali in a crowded living room, every Sunday evening at a temple in Houston or Leicester or Nairobi. Grandparents sing it loudly. Teenagers half-sing it. Everyone knows the first line. Yesterday you circled the flame. Today: the song that usually goes with it.
screen: `THE TUNE EVERYONE KNOWS.` → `LIVING ROOMS AND TEMPLES.` → `TODAY: THE ARTI SONG.`

segments.voice: The song is Om jai jagadish hare. It isn't ancient. It's usually credited to Shardha Ram Phillauri, a writer from Punjab, in the eighteen-seventies, and it's in Hindi, not Sanskrit, which is part of why it spread: anyone could understand it. Here's the first line, the one everybody knows: Om jai jagadish hare, swami jai jagadish hare. Let's open it word by word. Om, the first sound, your word from day two. Jai, victory, or glory, the word people shout at festivals. Jagadish is two words joined: jagat, the world, the moving universe, and ish, lord. The lord of the world. And hare calls on Hari, a name of Vishnu, the one who takes away. Swami means master, lord. So: Om, victory to you, lord of the world, O Hari. Victory, master, to the lord of the world. Then the verse goes on to say why: the troubles of your devotees, of those who serve you, you take away in a moment. That's the whole song in small. It isn't a request list. It starts with praise, jai, and only then remembers that people are hurting and trusts that help comes quickly. The song is addressed to Vishnu, but in many homes it's sung at the end of almost any puja, to whatever form is on the shelf. And it's sung while the flame circles: the tune and the light move together.
screen: `A SONG FROM THE 1870S, IN HINDI.` · `JAI — VICTORY, GLORY.` · `JAGAT + ISH: LORD OF THE WORLD.` · `PRAISE FIRST, THEN THE TROUBLES.`

segments.voice: Let's try it, slowly, even if singing isn't your thing. You can speak it, or just listen inside. Om jai jagadish hare. Swami jai jagadish hare. Once more, a little slower, and if you'd like, hold your flame or your open hand and let it circle with the tune. Om jai jagadish hare. Swami jai jagadish hare. Then let the sound stop and sit in what's left of it. If you don't pray, you can simply listen to what these words have meant to millions of kitchens. The bell holds the time.
Om jai jagadish hare. The arti song: Om, victory to you, lord of the world, O Hari. Today's word.
Your line: victory to the lord of the world. Today, before you ask for anything, start with one line of thanks or praise, and notice how the asking changes. Day one hundred and twenty.

121.title: Taking the light
121.howItsDone: At the end of arti, the lamp is brought to each person, who passes cupped hands over the flame without touching it and then touches the hands to the eyes, face or head; in temples, people often place a small offering on the plate as it passes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the arti song: Om jai jagadish hare. Your line was victory to the lord of the world. Did you start with thanks before asking for anything? Day one hundred and twenty-one.
screen: `OM JAI JAGADISH HARE — VICTORY TO THE LORD OF THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: The first time you go to arti with a Hindu friend, there's a moment that can catch you off guard. The song ends. The bell stops. And then the person holding the lamp turns around and walks toward you, holding out the plate with the flame still burning. Everyone near you does something with their hands, quickly, easily, like they've done it a thousand times, which they have. And you stand there wondering: am I supposed to touch it? Blow on it? Pass? Today, the moment after the song: taking the light.
screen: `THE SONG ENDS.` → `THE PLATE COMES TOWARD YOU.` → `WHAT DO YOU DO WITH YOUR HANDS?`

segments.voice: Here's what people are doing. When the arti plate reaches you, you cup your hands and pass them over the flame, close enough to feel the warmth, never touching. Then you draw your hands back toward yourself and bring them to your eyes, your face, sometimes over the top of your head. Many people do it twice or three times. Some use both hands. Some use only the right. That's it. It takes about three seconds. Why? The idea is simple and very old. The flame has just been circled before the divine. It has been, you might say, in the presence. Now it comes out to the people, and you take a little of that light and warmth and bring it into yourself: over the eyes, so you see well; over the head, as a blessing. Remember your fourteenth word, arti, and its line, light passed hand to hand. This is that line, literally. The light went to the shrine, and now it goes from palm to palm through the whole room. A few quiet customs travel with it. Many people don't blow out an arti flame; blowing on a sacred flame is seen as disrespectful, so it's left to burn down or put out another way. In temples, people often drop a coin or a small note on the plate as it passes. And if you're a guest and unsure, it's fine to watch first, then copy the person next to you. Nobody is keeping score. The light is offered to everyone in the room.
screen: `HANDS OVER THE FLAME, NOT TOUCHING.` · `BACK TO THE EYES, THE FACE, THE HEAD.` · `LIGHT PASSED HAND TO HAND.` · `DON'T BLOW IT OUT.`

segments.voice: If you have a candle or lamp and it's safe, light it and set it steady in front of you. If not, picture the arti plate coming toward you. Cup your hands. Pass them slowly over the warmth, a few inches above, never touching. Draw them back and rest your palms softly over your closed eyes. Feel the warmth there. Once more, and this time let your hands pass over the top of your head. Then rest your hands in your lap and stay with the flame. The bell holds the time.
Taking the light. After arti, hands pass over the flame and come back to the eyes and the head: the light from the shrine, taken into yourself. Today's word.
Your line: take it. Today, when something good is offered to you, a compliment, help, a kindness, don't wave it away. Take it. Day one hundred and twenty-one.

122.title: Family arti
122.howItsDone: In many Hindu homes, evening arti is a family gathering: one person circles the lamp, a child often rings the bell, everyone sings, and the lamp is passed around so each person can take the light.

segments.voice: Yesterday, taking the light: hands over the flame, then to the eyes. Your line was take it. Did you let someone's kindness land, without waving it away? Day one hundred and twenty-two.

Ask people who grew up with evening arti what they remember, and it's rarely the words. It's who was there. Dad holding the plate a little too high. A little sister fighting to ring the bell, and ringing it the entire time. An aunt singing half a beat ahead of everyone. The smell of camphor, and dinner waiting in the next room. For ten minutes, the whole house was facing the same way. This week you've learned the hour, the flame, the song and the light. All of it works alone. But arti was built for more than one. Today: family arti.
screen: `WHAT PEOPLE REMEMBER: WHO WAS THERE.` → `THE WHOLE HOUSE FACING ONE WAY.` → `TODAY: FAMILY ARTI.`

segments.voice: Look at how arti is put together and you'll see it almost asks for company. It has jobs. Someone holds the lamp. Someone rings the bell, often the youngest, because it's the best job. Everyone sings. Then the plate goes around, and each person takes the light. Even the smallest child has something to do. That's by design. Hindu tradition names four stages of life, and the second, the householder, grihastha, is the one lived in a home full of people. Many teachers have praised it as the stage that holds up the others, because the household is where the feeding, the raising, the caring for elders all happen. And the home shrine sits right in the middle of it. Worship isn't something you leave the house to do; the house is where it's done. So evening arti becomes a kind of daily meeting. The day's arguments get paused. The phones go down, or at least face down. For ten minutes, whoever is under that roof stands together in front of one flame. Now, real families are complicated. Some people live alone. Some live with a partner from another faith, or with none. Nobody here is saying anyone has to join. A guest can simply stand in the room, listen and watch. But the invitation matters. People say you can pray alone anywhere. Arti, done together, adds something else. It's one of the ways a house becomes a home.
screen: `ARTI HAS JOBS: LAMP, BELL, SONG.` · `THE HOUSEHOLDER: GRIHASTHA.` · `THE HOUSE IS WHERE IT'S DONE.` · `NO ONE HAS TO. EVERYONE IS ASKED.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Bring to mind one person you could invite to do this with you, even once. A roommate, a parent on a video call, a partner, a child, a friend. Picture them in the room with you: one of you holds the flame, one rings the bell. Notice how it feels to not be the only one facing the light. Then think of how you might ask them, simply, with no pressure at all. If they say no, that's fine too. The bell holds the time.
Family arti. Arti done together: one lamp, one bell, one song, and a job for everyone in the house. Today's word.
Your line: one more. Today, ask one more person to join something you usually do alone: a walk, a meal, a minute of quiet, the flame. Day one hundred and twenty-two.

123.title: Sunset without objects
123.hook: arti with nothing but the actual sun
123.howItsDone: Many Hindus honor the sun directly, pouring water toward it at dawn or bowing to it at the twilight junctions; when no shrine is available, some simply face the rising or setting sun with folded hands.

segments.voice: Yesterday, family arti: a job for everyone in the house. Your line was one more. Did you ask one more person to join something? Day one hundred and twenty-three.

You're in a hospital waiting room. Or an airport. Or a dorm where candles are banned, or a friend's house, or a work trip in a hotel with a window that doesn't open. No shelf, no lamp, no bell, no flower. It's evening, and the part of you that has started to expect arti this week feels a little lost. So here's today's question. If you took away every object from this week, the lamp, the plate, the camphor, the song sheet, what would be left? There's an old answer. Look out the window. Today: sunset without objects.
screen: `NO SHELF, NO LAMP, NO BELL.` → `WHAT'S LEFT?` → `LOOK OUT THE WINDOW.`

segments.voice: Long before there were brass lamps and printed arti songs, there were the Vedas, the oldest Hindu scriptures. And the very first hymn of the Rig Veda is to Agni, fire, praised as the priest of the sacrifice, the one who carries offerings to the gods. Many of the hymns that follow sing to the dawn, and to the sun. The Gayatri, from day one hundred and eight, asks the light of the sun to wake up the mind. The sun has a special title in Hindu tradition: people call it the god you can actually see. You don't need an image to imagine it; it's right there, every day, rising and setting. So think about the arti lamp this way. Every evening, as the sun goes down, a household lights a small flame and holds it up. The little flame is a kind of stand-in for the big one, carried indoors for the night. The sun is the original flame. And that means, when you have nothing, you still have it. Many Hindus pour water toward the sun at dawn. At dusk, you can simply turn west, where the sun is setting, put your hands together, and watch. That's the whole ritual: the light that circled the earth all day, finishing its circle in front of you. One practical thing. Never stare straight into the sun. Watch the sky around it, the colors, the edges of the clouds. The light will find your face without your help.
screen: `THE RIG VEDA OPENS WITH FIRE.` · `THE GOD YOU CAN ACTUALLY SEE.` · `THE LAMP IS A STAND-IN.` · `FACE WEST. HANDS TOGETHER. WATCH.`

segments.voice: If you can, turn toward the west, toward a window, or where the sun sets even if it's hidden right now. If it's not evening, picture the last sunset you remember well. Put your hands together at your chest, if you'd like. Don't look at the sun itself; look at the sky around it. Let the color be the flame, and the whole horizon be the plate. Nothing to hold. Nothing to light. Just the original flame, and you in front of it. The bell holds the time.
Sunset without objects. Arti with nothing but the actual sun: face west, hands together, and watch the original flame go down. Today's word.
Your line: the original flame. Today, wherever you are at sunset, stop for one minute and face it. No objects needed. Day one hundred and twenty-three.

124.title: Your evening routine
124.hook: assemble: bell, breath, arti, one line
124.howItsDone: Many Hindu households close the day with evening arti at the home shrine, often with a bell, the circled lamp, a song or mantra, and a closing invocation of peace such as Om shanti shanti shanti.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sunset without objects: just the sun, and you facing it. Your line was the original flame. Did you catch a sunset, even a gray one? Day one hundred and twenty-four.

Look at this week. It began with sandhya, the hour where day and night join. Then arti at home, a small flame circled. Om jai jagadish hare, the song everyone knows. Taking the light, hands over the flame to your eyes. Family arti, one more person in the room. And yesterday, the sun itself. Last week you built a morning. This week, the other end of the day. Because most of us don't end the day. We just stop. The phone falls on our face at midnight. Today we build the other bookend: your evening routine.
screen: `A WEEK OF DUSK.` → `MOST DAYS DON'T END, THEY STOP.` → `TODAY: THE OTHER BOOKEND.`

segments.voice: Here's a shape. Four pieces, about five minutes, built only from things you already know. First, the bell. One ring, and follow it all the way to silence. That's arriving, from day one hundred and fourteen. Second, the breath. You learned it back in week fifteen: in for four, out for six. A few rounds of the longer out-breath tell the body the day is closing. Third, arti. If you have a lamp, light it and circle it slowly, maybe humming the first line of the song. If you don't, face the window, toward where the sun went down. Then take the light: hands over the flame, back to your eyes. And fourth, one line. Many Hindu prayers close the same way, with Om and three shantis. Om shanti, shanti, shanti. Your fourth word, peace, peace, peace. Some people use their own mantra here instead. Just one line, said slowly, as the last thing. Bell, breath, arti, one line. That's it. Now notice what this routine is for. The morning puja offers the day before it starts. The evening routine hands the day back. Whatever happened, the good meeting, the argument, the thing you forgot, you don't have to carry it into sleep. People in many traditions have a way of closing the day. This is one Hindu way: a flame, a breath, a word of peace, and the day put down.
screen: `THE BELL: ARRIVE.` · `THE BREATH: LONGER OUT.` · `ARTI: THE FLAME, OR THE WINDOW.` · `ONE LINE: OM SHANTI, SHANTI, SHANTI.`

segments.voice: Let's do it now, all four. Ring your bell, or tap a glass, and follow the sound to silence. Now breathe in for four, out for six. Twice more. If you have a flame, circle it slowly, clockwise, and take the light to your eyes; if not, turn toward the window. Then, quietly, if you'd like: Om shanti, shanti, shanti. Now name one thing from today, just one, and set it down. The bell holds the time.
Your evening routine. Bell, breath, arti, one line: five minutes that close the day instead of letting it just stop. Today's word.
Your line: the day put down. Tonight, before your phone, do the four pieces, even in a shortened version. That's the week. Tomorrow we turn to the body. Day one hundred and twenty-four.

125.title: The body as temple
125.howItsDone: Many Hindus bathe before morning puja and treat bodily care, food, rest and movement as part of religious life, drawing on the idea, found in later Upanishads and in devotional poetry, that the body is a temple in which the divine dwells.

segments.voice: Yesterday, your evening routine: bell, breath, arti, one line. Your line was the day put down. Did you close the day, or did it just stop? Day one hundred and twenty-five.
screen: `YOUR EVENING ROUTINE — THE DAY PUT DOWN.`

segments.voice: For two weeks you've been building a shrine. A corner, a shelf, a lamp, a flower, a bell, a cup of water. You've learned to keep it clean, to bring fresh flowers, to light it at the edges of the day. Now look down. At your hands. Your feet. The chest going up and down. There's a shrine you've been carrying around this whole time, one you didn't have to buy, and most of us treat it worse than the shelf. We skip its meals, cut its sleep, and only notice it when it hurts. A new week starts today, about the body and food. Today: the body as temple.
screen: `TWO WEEKS BUILDING A SHRINE.` → `NOW LOOK DOWN.` → `TODAY: THE BODY AS TEMPLE.`

segments.voice: There's a short line in one of the later Upanishads, the Maitreya Upanishad, that says it straight out: the body is called a temple, and the living one inside it is Shiva himself. The body is the building. What lives in it is holy. You met that idea on day ten, atman: someone is in there. Today's day asks what that means for the building. A twelfth-century poet-saint from Karnataka, Basavanna, said it in a poem people still sing. The rich, he says, build temples for Shiva. What can a poor man do? Then he answers: my legs are the pillars, my body is the shrine, my head is the golden dome. He didn't need stone. He was already standing in one. Here's why this matters on an ordinary Tuesday. If the body is a temple, then looking after it isn't vanity, and it isn't a chore separate from the spiritual life. Bathing before puja, eating with some care, sleeping enough, moving, resting: these become part of the practice, the way sweeping the shrine is part of puja. And notice what the idea doesn't say. It doesn't say the temple has to be perfect, young or strong. A temple can be old. It can be cracked, patched, or hard to climb the steps of. Bodies that are sick, tired, disabled or aging are still temples, and still lived in. The point isn't how it looks. The point is who lives there. This week is about caring for the building.
screen: `THE BODY IS CALLED A TEMPLE.` · `BASAVANNA: MY LEGS ARE THE PILLARS.` · `CARE IS PART OF THE PRACTICE.` · `A TEMPLE CAN BE OLD, OR CRACKED.`

segments.voice: Sit or lie down, whatever's kinder today. Close your eyes if you like. Start at your feet, the foundation. Just notice them. Move up: the legs, Basavanna's pillars. The belly, moving with the breath. The chest. The hands, which did so much work today. The shoulders, where the day usually hides. The face. The top of the head, the dome. Don't fix anything. Just visit each part, the way you'd walk slowly through a temple. This is where you live. The bell holds the time.
The body as temple. The old idea that the body is a shrine and someone holy lives in it, so caring for it is part of the practice. Today's word.
Your line: this is where you live. Today, do one small kind thing for the building: a glass of water, a stretch, going to bed a little earlier. Day one hundred and twenty-five.

126.title: Sun salutation, plainly
126.howItsDone: Many Hindus practice surya namaskar in the morning, facing east, as both exercise and devotion, sometimes reciting one of the twelve names of the sun, such as Om Mitraya namah, with each round.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the body as temple. Your line was this is where you live. What small kind thing did you do for the building? Day one hundred and twenty-six.
screen: `THE BODY AS TEMPLE — THIS IS WHERE YOU LIVE.`

segments.voice: If you've ever taken a yoga class, you've probably done it. Arms up. Fold forward. Step back. Down, up, dog, forward, rise. The instructor calls it a sun salutation, the music is soft, and everyone is mostly worried about their hamstrings. Nobody mentions the sun. But the name is telling you something. It isn't called the stretch sequence. It's a salutation, a greeting, and it's addressed to someone. Yesterday you walked slowly through the temple of the body. Today you move it, and point it at the oldest flame there is. Today: sun salutation, plainly.

segments.voice: Surya namaskar. Surya is the sun, the god you can actually see, from day one hundred and twenty-three. Namaskar is a bow, from the same root as namaste, your very first word. So: a bow to the sun. In its common form it's a flowing loop of about twelve positions. Stand with palms together. Reach up. Fold forward. Step one leg back into a lunge. Come into a plank, lower down, lift the chest. Push back into a mountain shape, step forward, fold, reach up, and return to standing, palms together. Each movement goes with a breath, in as you open, out as you fold. Many people who practice it as devotion add something the gym leaves out: one of the twelve names of the sun, said with each round. The first is Om Mitraya namah: a bow to Mitra, the friend. Now, plainly, the history. Honoring the sun is ancient in India; the Gayatri and the Vedic hymns are full of it. Bowing to the sun at dawn is old too. But the exact flowing sequence taught in classes around the world was shaped and made popular quite recently, in the early twentieth century, by a raja in western India who promoted it for health. Both things are true. It's an old devotion wearing a fairly new shape. And so it can be two things at once: exercise, and a bow. Many Hindus do it every morning, facing east, as both. What makes it a salutation is the direction you face, and who you have in mind.

segments.voice: A gentle version, three rounds. Skip anything that hurts; you can do it seated, just moving your arms. Stand, or sit tall, facing east if you know where it is. Palms together at your chest. Breathe in, reach up. Breathe out, fold forward as far as is comfortable. Breathe in, lift halfway. Breathe out, fold. Breathe in, rise all the way up, arms high. Breathe out, palms back to the chest. That's one. Twice more, slowly. If you'd like, say the friend's name with each round. Then sit, and feel the warmth. The bell holds the time.
Surya namaskar. A bow to the sun: a flowing loop of positions, one breath each, done as exercise, as devotion, or both. Today's word.
Your line: bow to the sun. Tomorrow morning, before anything else, face the light for one round, even just arms up and palms together. Day one hundred and twenty-six.

trapdoor: what you thought: a yoga warm-up.
what it means: a bow to the sun, a loop of positions with a breath each, which many Hindus practice as both exercise and devotion.

what a scholar hears: the modern twelve-position sequence was popularized in the 1920s by Bhawanrao Shriniwasrao Pant Pratinidhi, Raja of Aundh, drawing on older practices of solar worship and prostration; the twelve names begin with Mitra.
